lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Git & Contribution Basics
lessons.description: Branching, issue linking, and how you actually find a first issue.

questions.prompt: Which command creates a new feature branch and switches to it in one step?

options.text: git branch fix/issue-10
git checkout -b fix/issue-10
git commit -m 'fix issue'
git push origin main

questions.explanation: `git checkout -b fix/issue-10` (or `git switch -c`) creates the branch and checks it out. `git branch` only creates it; you would still need to switch.

questions.prompt: In a pull request body, how do you link the work to GitHub issue 42 so the issue can close when the PR merges?

options.text: Write the issue number only: 42
Use a closing keyword: Fixes #42
Tag @github
Put the issue URL in a commit that never gets pushed

questions.explanation: `Fixes #42`, `Closes #42`, or `Resolves #42` links the PR to the issue and can auto-close it on merge.

questions.prompt: You want beginner issues in Python on GitHub. Which search is the most useful starting point?

options.text: stars:>100000 is:closed
language:python label:"good first issue" state:open
filename:password.txt
org:ghost

questions.explanation: Filter by language plus a newcomer label and open state. Huge starred + closed searches hide the work you can actually take.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that belongs in a first contribution.

options.text: Read README and CONTRIBUTING before writing code.
Work on a branch, not on upstream main.
Force-push to the project's main branch.
Comment on the issue before (or as) you start, if the project asks you to.

questions.explanation: Read the room, branch off main, talk to maintainers. Never force-push someone else's default branch.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: Conflicts & History
lessons.description: Conflict markers, rebase vs merge, and what not to rewrite.

questions.prompt: You open a file after a failed merge and see <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. What should you do?

options.text: Commit immediately; Git already picked a winner.
Edit the file to the intended result, delete the markers, then add and commit.
Delete the repository and clone again.
Run git push --force on main.

questions.explanation: Conflict markers are a pause, not a result. You choose the code, remove the markers, then stage and commit the resolution.

questions.prompt: When is `git rebase` a reasonable tool on your own feature branch?

options.text: To replay your commits on top of latest main before you open a PR.
To rewrite commits already on the shared main branch.
To delete GitHub issues.
To skip code review.

questions.explanation: Rebase your unpushed (or solo) feature branch onto updated main. Do not rebase public history others already pulled.

questions.prompt: Select the true statements.

options.text: git fetch updates your remote-tracking branches without merging.
A merge commit records that two histories were joined.
git push --force on origin/main is standard for first-time contributors.
Small, focused commits are easier to review than one giant dump.

questions.explanation: Fetch is safe. Merge commits are a record. Force-pushing main is how you become unwelcome. Small diffs review faster.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Pull Requests
lessons.description: What a reviewable PR looks like.

questions.prompt: A reviewable first PR usually is:

options.text: A rewrite of the entire codebase.
Small, tested, and described, with the related issue linked.
Pushed straight to upstream main.
Opened without a description so reviewers 'see the code'.

questions.explanation: Maintainers merge small, explained changes. Giant surprise rewrites stall.

questions.prompt: CI on your PR is red. Best next move?

options.text: Ask for merge anyway; CI is optional.
Read the failing job, fix it on your branch, and push a follow-up commit.
Close the repo.
Open five more PRs to distract from it.

questions.explanation: Green checks are part of the contribution. Fix the branch; don't argue with the required workflow.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about review.

options.text: Review comments are normal; reply and/or push fixes.
You should discuss scope on the issue if the fix grows.
Changing files the issue never mentioned, silently, is a gift.
A polite, specific PR description saves a round of questions.

questions.explanation: Review is collaboration. Stay on scope unless you agree otherwise. Write like a teammate.

lessons.title: Assessment: Mentorship Programs
lessons.description: Pick the right program for the right person — and the work that has to happen first.

questions.prompt: The strongest GSoC / LFX / Outreachy application usually includes:

options.text: Zero prior PRs and a very long essay.
Merged (or at least serious) contributions to the org, plus a specific proposal.
A promise to learn the language after selection only.
Copy-pasting last year's winning proposal unchanged.

questions.explanation: Mentors pick people they have already seen in the issue tracker. Proof of work beats a generic essay.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is most accurate?

options.text: Outreachy is only for people who already completed GSoC.
LFX Mentorship is run around Linux Foundation / CNCF-style projects in seasonal terms.
GSoC still requires you to be enrolled in a university.
All three programs merge your PRs without a mentor.

questions.explanation: LFX is the LF/CNCF mentorship board. GSoC has not required student status since 2022. Outreachy has its own eligibility (underrepresented in tech) and a contribution phase. Always read the current year's rules.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement.

options.text: Read this year's official timeline; dates move.
Pick 1–2 orgs and show up in their chat/issues early.
You can skip CONTRIBUTING.md if the stipend is large.
A proposal should name a project, a mentor-facing plan, and a realistic schedule.

questions.explanation: Timelines change. Depth beats spraying 20 orgs. Proposals are project plans, not vibes. Process docs still apply.

courses.title: Building Your Own Product: Idea to Launch

courses.description: A practical, video-based path for builders: find a problem worth solving, talk to real users, scope the smallest version worth shipping, and launch it — then do it again.

lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Idea & Validation
lessons.description: Evaluating an idea and running a real user interview.

questions.prompt: Per YC's framework for evaluating startup ideas, which is the strongest signal an idea is worth pursuing?

options.text: It sounds impressive when you pitch it at a party.
You (or people you know) genuinely need this and would use it today.
No one has ever tried anything like it.
It requires the least possible work to build.

questions.explanation: YC favors founders solving a problem they deeply understand and already feel, not an idea that merely sounds novel or easy.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of an early user interview?

options.text: Convince the user your idea is good.
Understand their current behavior and pain points without pitching your solution.
Get them to pre-pay immediately.
Ask only yes/no questions to save time.

questions.explanation: Good interviews focus on understanding existing behavior and pain. Pitching too early biases the feedback you get.

questions.prompt: Select every section that belongs on a Lean Canvas.

options.text: Problem
Unique Value Proposition
Office lease terms
Key Metrics

questions.explanation: The Lean Canvas covers problem, solution, UVP, channels, customer segments, cost structure, revenue, key metrics, and unfair advantage — not operational details like a lease.

modules.title: Week 2: Scoping and Shipping an MVP
modules.summary: Turn a validated idea into the smallest version worth building — and say it out loud clearly.

lessons.title: Michael Seibel - How to Plan an MVP
lessons.description: What actually counts as an MVP, and why 'launch something bad quickly' beats a long, quiet build.

lessons.title: Kevin Hale - How to Pitch Your Startup
lessons.description: Package the idea into a pitch: the initial conditions, the solution, and the insight for why it can work — useful for users, cofounders, or investors alike.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: MVP & Pitch
lessons.description: Scoping an MVP and framing a pitch.

questions.prompt: Per Michael Seibel's MVP framework, what should your first MVP optimize for?

options.text: Supporting every feature you can imagine.
The smallest thing you can ship to test if you can deliver real value to a few users.
A polished, investor-ready product.
Building for a huge, general audience from day one.

questions.explanation: Seibel's advice: launch something ridiculously simple to a narrow set of early users first, then iterate on what you learn.

questions.prompt: In Kevin Hale's pitch framework, a startup idea is best understood as:

options.text: A finished business plan.
A hypothesis about why the company could grow quickly, made of initial conditions, solution, and insight.
A guaranteed outcome once funded.
Only relevant once you have paying customers.

questions.explanation: Hale frames a pitch as a hypothesis: why this solution, at this moment, for this insight, could grow fast.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that matches 'launch something bad quickly' thinking.

options.text: Ship a limited version to a small set of users this week.
Delay launch until every edge case is handled.
Treat the first release as a way to learn, not a finished product.
Talk to the first users again after they try it.

questions.explanation: MVP thinking favors fast, narrow releases you learn from, not indefinite polishing before anyone sees it.

modules.title: Week 3: Launching & Getting First Users
modules.summary: Ship it publicly, then do it again.

lessons.title: Kat Mañalac - How to Launch (Again and Again)
lessons.description: Why launching is a continuous process — silent launch, friends & family, launching to strangers, and building your own community.

lessons.title: How to Launch on Product Hunt (Official Guide)
lessons.description: Product Hunt's own walkthrough of preparing for and running a launch day.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Launching
lessons.description: Launching as a repeatable process, not a one-time event.

questions.prompt: Per 'How to Launch (Again and Again)', launching is best treated as:

options.text: A single, one-time event on launch day.
A continuous process you repeat for every meaningful update.
Something to avoid until the product is perfect.
Only relevant for consumer apps.

questions.explanation: The core point: launch repeatedly — silent launch, friends & family, strangers, press — not just once.

questions.prompt: Per Product Hunt's official launch guide, which practice most improves a launch?

options.text: Submitting with no prior engagement on the platform.
Participating in the community and building relationships before launch day.
Launching without a live product URL.
Avoiding all outside promotion.

questions.explanation: Product Hunt recommends genuine, sustained participation (comments, upvotes, feedback) well before your own launch, not a cold submission.

questions.prompt: Select every legitimate way to 'launch again' for an existing product.

options.text: Announcing a major new feature.
Re-launching to a new audience or platform.
Reposting the exact same launch post daily.
Sharing a milestone (users, revenue, an integration) as its own moment.

questions.explanation: Each real update, audience, or milestone is a legitimate reason to launch again — spamming the same post isn't.
